history.period: 11th-12th century CE (inscriptions at the site dated 1153-1178 CE)
history.summary: A group of ruined Hindu temples at Kiradu village in the Thar Desert, about 35 km from Barmer - CSV town 'Barmer' is approximate; the town field below names Kiradu. Of the five surviving structures, the Someshvara temple (Shiva) is the best preserved: its surviving walls, columns and sculpture are enough to reconstruct the design, though the shikhara has collapsed and the mandapa roof is largely gone. The temples are built in the Maru-Gurjara (Solanki-mode) style, famed for erotic and sensuous carving, which earns the site the nickname 'Khajuraho of Rajasthan'. Inscriptions dated 1153-1178 CE support a 12th-century date (Gaurishankar Ojha, Ratna Chandra Agrawala, Stella Kramrisch); Madhusudan Dhaky and Percy Brown assigned them to the 11th century. Kiradu was originally known as Kiratakupa/Kiradkot, a capital of Panwar/Paramara rulers on Thar trade routes; a Paramara chief Someshvara rose here in the 1140s CE under Chaulukya favour, and an 1178 CE inscription records repairs to a temple damaged by the Turushkas (identified with Muhammad of Ghor's Ghurids). The ruins have been restored by the Archaeological Survey of India and are ASI-protected (per tourism sources; the ASI notification was not independently verified in this pass).
